newsitem.title: UK: Test-tube cells help treat damaged eyes in Italy.
newsitem.headline: Test-tube cells help treat damaged eyes in Italy.

text.p: Italian researchers reported on Friday they had managed to grow eye cells in a laboratory dish and use them to treat people with damaged corneas.
They said the technique could greatly help doctors trying to help people with damaged or diseased corneas.

Dr Michele de Luca and colleagues at the Istituto Dermopatico dell'Immacolata in Rome first grew corneal tissue in a laboratory. Having established the procedure, they took tiny samples from the healthy eyes of two volunteers who each had one eye badly damaged by chemical burns.

They grew these cultures over a soft contact lens so they would take on the right shape, then transplanted them on to the injured eyes of each patient. Both worked, they reported in the Lancet medical journal.

The first volunteer, aged 62, had been nearly blinded by a chemical burn and could barely see hand movements. The second, 39, had undergone grafts from his good eye before but they did not work. He could barely see. "At the last follow-up (more than two years after grafting), both patients were clinically stable," De Luca's group wrote.

Indications were that the damaged corneas had re-generated, and that cells known as stem cells, which can divide and form different kinds of cells depending on what is needed, were working properly. De Luca said the procedure could offer an alternative to patients who have damaged one eye and do not want to risk losing tissue from the good eye for a transplant.
It could offer the first hope of surgery to patients who have damaged or disease in both eyes.
